```{r}
#| label: original-study

# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. 
#
# Jara-Ettinger & Rubio-Fernandez (2021), Experiment 1 (N = 60): Each participant's performance
# on the belief inference task was compared against a theory of mind model (Model A) and a deductive model (Model B)
# The subject-level difference is tested with a paired t test. (Page 4, Paragraph 4)
original <- list(
  n = 60,   # number of participants in the paired test
  t = 5.43,    # paired t statistic, Model A vs Model B
  mean_diff = 0.24 # mean difference between correlation of Model A and Model B
)
original_dz <- original$t / sqrt(original$n)
```

# Key statistics

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the
analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered
exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the Phase 2 row reports the new comparison:
adapt its code and say so in the caption.
:::

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusion rule: analyze everyone who finished the study and has all 14 trials saved.
  # The original experiment data contain only complete sessions and report no exclusions.
  n_main <- trials |>
    filter(task == "trial") |>
    count(participant_id, name = "n_main_trials")
  keep <- complete |>
    left_join(n_main, by = "participant_id") |>
    filter(n_main_trials %in% 14)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep)
}

# Model predictions for the 28 trials, from the authors' OSF archive (osf.io/h8qfy,
# ProcessedData/Exp1_Model.csv): "ToM" is Model A, "Deductive" is Model B. Same coordinates as
# the trackpads: x = probability of the right column, y = probability of the bottom row;
# lref = display A, rref = display B, cg = blind spot.
model_predictions <- read_csv(file.path("..", "data", "original", "Exp1_Model.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(lref_x:cg_y, names_to = "variable") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value)

# How well one participant's responses fit one model: as in the original's subject-level
# analysis (Exp1_AnalyzeResults.R), the correlation across that participant's 14 trials
# between their trackpad positions (x and y, so 28 values) and the model's predictions.
score_fit <- function(response, prediction) cor(response, prediction, use = "complete.obs")

# Each analyzed participant's fit to Model A and Model B, and the difference (A - B), for
# belief (blind spot) inferences, the cg_x and cg_y trackpad. Responses are already in the
# model's orientation (experiment.js undoes the rotation and left/right swap). Participants
# whose fit can't be computed (e.g. the blind-spot marker never moved) are dropped here.
# Run on the original participants' data, this reproduces the paper: 0.586 vs 0.350, t(59) = 5.43.
participant_scores <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "trial", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    select(participant_id, TrialId = trial_id, cg_x, cg_y) |>
    pivot_longer(c(cg_x, cg_y), names_to = "variable", values_to = "response") |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(score_a = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, ToM)),
              score_b = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, Deductive)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(!is.na(score_a), !is.na(score_b)) |>
    mutate(diff = score_a - score_b)
}

# The key statistic: mean paired difference (Model A minus Model B) with a 95% CI, the
# paired t test, and d_z. NULL until at least two participants have scores.
paired_test <- function(scores) {
  if (is.null(scores) || nrow(scores) < 2) return(NULL)
  tt <- t.test(scores$score_a, scores$score_b, paired = TRUE)
  tibble(N = nrow(scores),
         estimate  = unname(tt$estimate),
         ci_low    = tt$conf.int[1], ci_high = tt$conf.int[2],
         statistic = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter), p = tt$p.value,
         d_z       = mean(scores$diff) / sd(scores$diff))
}

# The original study's paired difference and 95% CI, rebuilt from its reported mean
# difference, paired t, and N, in the same shape paired_test() returns.
original_paired <- function(o) {
  df   <- o$n - 1
  se   <- abs(o$mean_diff / o$t)
  half <- qt(0.975, df) * se
  tibble(N = o$n, estimate = o$mean_diff,
         ci_low = o$mean_diff - half, ci_high = o$mean_diff + half,
         statistic = o$t, df = df, p = 2 * pt(-abs(o$t), df),
         d_z = o$t / sqrt(o$n))
}

# Side-by-side figure: each study's paired difference with its 95% CI, in the order given.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, is.null)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", N))
  cols <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Study, y = estimate, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), size = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(y = ci_high, label = label), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "ToM minus deductive model\n(per-participant r, belief inferences)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Difference (A − B)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", `t (df)` = "", p = "", `d_z` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Difference (A − B)` = sprintf("%.3f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         `t (df)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.0f)", r$statistic, r$df),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         `d_z` = sprintf("%.2f", r$d_z))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original_paired(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) paired_test(participant_scores(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) paired_test(participant_scores(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrllllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: mean per-participant difference in fit to Model A minus Model B, paired t test.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
In this project, I tried to replicate Experiment 1 of Jara-Ettinger & Rubio-Fernandez (2021). The original study found that adults can infer what information speakers know about objects based on the specificity of the language they use to refer to them. In Experiment 1, participants were shown four shapes on a screen and then told that speakers could not see one of the four objects and to guess what the speaker was referring to and what the speaker's blind spot was. They found that adults' predictions about which of the four shapes speakers did not know was better predicted by a theory of mind model that inferred speakers' knowledge from the specificity of their reference, than a deductive model that did not. The key statistic I aimed to replicate was that participants' belief predictions were better predicted by the theory of mind model compared to the deductive model (*t*(59) = 5.43, *p* < 0.0001 by paired *t* test) 

This finding mattered to me since I am interested in thinking about frameworks to use to understand how children reason about speaker beliefs to learn words. To aid in that goal, I extended this study by replacing the speaker object reference with a 2-3 sentence long conversational segment inspired by CHILDES, a naturalistic corpus of what children hear, and replaced the objects with real-world objects that could be referred to across these segments.

## Methods

### Power analysis

The original effect size found was 0.70. Details about the number of participants required to detect that effect with different amounts of power are detailed below.

```{r}
#| label: power
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_dz, sd = 1, power = pw,
                    sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n = ceiling(n))
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N participants"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Participants needed to detect the original Model A vs Model B difference (d_z = %.2f), paired t test, two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original_dz))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half[1]` in total. I chose a sample size of 20 to be able to detect the original effect size with at least 80% power.

### Planned sample

I planned to collect a sample size of 20. Those participants were required to be US residents on Prolific who were fluent in English and 18 or older. I collected data until 20 participants passed the exclusion criteria below.

### Materials

Tutorial: "Participants first read a brief tutorial and had to complete a small questionnaire to ensure they
read the instructions. See our OSF site for screenshots of the tutorial, inclusion
questionnaire, and test screen." Instructions pages 6, 7, 8, and 9 were updated to remove the 'Continue' button in the screenshots of the study to avoid confusion with the JS-Psych version of the 'Continue' button used that looks slightly different. The inclusion questionnaire was adapted into JS-Psych but had the same list of questions.

Shapes: "Stimuli consisted of 28 trials. Each trial in turn consisted of two 2 × 2 grids with four colored geometrical shapes and a definite description of one of them. Displays were created by combining 4 shapes (circle, square, triangle and star) in 4 colors (red, green, blue and yellow). We generated 4 possible conditions for each display by crossing the
presence or absence of a color adjective in the target description with the presence or absence of
a contrast shape in the display" The original authors provided information about each of the 28 trials (display combinations and utterance) on OSF that were used to design the stimuli for this study. Since the original authors did not provide the shapes themselves, I recreated these shapes as SVG objects based on how these objects appeared in the test screen screenshot. 

### Procedure

Participants first consented to participating in the study. Then, participants had to "read a brief tutorial and had to complete a small questionnaire to ensure they read the instructions. Participants who got at least one question wrong were redirected to the beginning of the tutorial and only participants who responded to all questions correctly were
allowed to participate in the study." 

Each participant saw 14 trials as part of the study. "Stimuli were randomly split into two subsets of 14 trials, and participants were presented with only one of the two lists" "Each trial in turn consisted of two 2 × 2 grids with four colored geometrical shapes and a definite description of one of them." "In each trial, participants were told that the speaker intended to refer to only one of the corners and that the speaker could not see one of the four corners. Participants were also told that the speaker could not see the same corner in each display. The speaker’s choice of referential expression to single out the target was written above each display. Trial order was randomized across participants. The pairs of displays were randomly ordered and rotated in each trial. In each trial, participants were presented with three 'trackpads,' each with a circle that the participants could position anywhere they wished. Participants had to input their belief about the referent in each display in the first two trackpads and their beliefs about the blind spot in the third trackpad." 

After the trials, participants were asked how old they were, to match the demographic data collected in the original study. On the next screen, participants were asked to optionally provide any comments they have. Finally, participants were shown a debrief screen where the purpose of the experiment is explained and it is disclosed that the speaker was simulated. 

The study took 20 minutes in total.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** Participants' performance on the belief task has a higher correlation with a theory-of-mind model as compared to a deductive model, tested with a paired t-test comparing the per-participant correlation difference. The effect size is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences, with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants will be excluded if they do not complete the study. Since the original experiment only contained participants with complete data, I added the first criterion to ensure that standard was matched.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | Adults recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk | Adults recruited on Prolific residing in the United States who speak English | Unlikely, the task uses shapes and no context-specific items and both samples are collected online. |
| Instructions | 'Continue' button in task design screenshot | No 'Continue' button in task design screenshot | Unlikely. The presence of the button is not relevant to understanding of the task design. |
| Exclusion criteria | None | Participants are excluded if they do not complete the study. | Unlikely, since all of the participants in the original sample had complete data. |
| Additional tasks | None | Participants are asked to provide their age and any additional comments | Unlikely. These tasks are only asked to be completed after the participant completes the experimental trials. |

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Belief inferences: each participant's correlation with Model A (ToM) vs Model B (deductive),
# paired t test (original: 0.586 vs 0.350, t(59) = 5.43).
scores <- participant_scores(phase1)
key    <- paired_test(scores)

if (!is.null(key)) {
  print(t.test(scores$score_a, scores$score_b, paired = TRUE))
  scores |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean r, Model A (ToM)` = mean(score_a),
              `Mean r, Model B (deductive)` = mean(score_b),
              `Model A fits better` = sum(diff > 0)) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Per-participant correlations with each model, belief inferences.")
} else {
  message("Paired t test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants with a computable ",
          "correlation; there are ", nrow(scores), ".")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_paired(original)
rep  <- key

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference in r (A − B)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              d_z = sprintf("%.2f", d_z),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: mean per-participant difference in correlation with Model A (ToM) and Model B (deductive), belief inferences.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Mean per-participant difference in correlation with Model A (ToM) and Model B (deductive), belief inferences, original study and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals; the original CIs are rebuilt from the reported statistics."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = orig, `Phase 1: replication` = key)
```

```{r}
  message("No errors were reported from participants' browsers.")
}
```

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the

:::

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same

:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n <- 150   # planned analysed participants in Phase 2 (each scored against both models)

p1_scores <- if (have_data) participant_scores(phase1)
p1_stats  <- if (have_data) paired_test(p1_scores)
orig      <- original_paired(original)

# SD of the per-participant differences, which sets precision. Taken from Phase 1 if it has
# data, otherwise recovered from the original's mean difference and t.
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(sd_diff = sd(p1_scores$diff), source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(sd_diff = abs(original$mean_diff) * sqrt(original$n) / abs(original$t),
       source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the mean difference with n participants.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, n - 1) * basis$sd_diff / sqrt(n)
power_at <- function(n, dz) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = abs(dz), sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05,
                        type = "paired")$power,
           error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, phase2_n),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.3f", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.3f (expected)", half_width(phase2_n)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate (Model A minus Model B), Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: d_z = %.2f", orig$d_z),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: d_z = %.2f", p1_stats$d_z),
                         sprintf("Half the original: d_z = %.2f", orig$d_z / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n, orig$d_z),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n, p1_stats$d_z),
    power_at(phase2_n, orig$d_z / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 paired t test at %d participants, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n))
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

The confirmatory analysis for Phase 2, written before Phase 2 data collection. On the

alone; say whether you will also report a pooled estimate across phases, and label it
exploratory if so. On the scientific track, specify the test for the new comparison. Name the

Run Phase 2 under a new `EXPERIMENT.id` in `experiment.js` (for example `smith2016-phase2`) and

```{r}
#| label: phase2-results
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
p2_stats <- paired_test(participant_scores(phase2))
cat(sprintf("Phase 2: %d started, %d completed, %d analysed.\n",
            nrow(phase2$participants), nrow(phase2$complete), nrow(phase2$keep)))
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {
  p_text <- if (p2_stats$p < 0.001) "p < .001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", p2_stats$p)
  cat(sprintf("Key comparison: difference in r = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], t(%.0f) = %.2f, %s.\n",
              p2_stats$estimate, p2_stats$ci_low, p2_stats$ci_high,
              p2_stats$df, p2_stats$statistic, p_text))
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8

comparison_plot(Original = original_paired(original),
                `Phase 1: replication` = if (have_data) paired_test(participant_scores(phase1)),
                `Phase 2: extension` = p2_stats)
```
